bib.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools

question: Can a language model teach itself, without large human annotation, to decide which APIs to call, when, with what arguments, and how to use the results?
hypothesis: Self-supervised finetuning on API calls kept only when they reduce future-token loss lets a small LM use tools and beat much larger models zero-shot without hurting language modeling.
contributions: Self-supervised method: sample API calls with in-context prompting, execute, filter by loss reduction, finetune
Five tools: QA (Atlas), calculator, Wikipedia BM25 search, NLLB translation, calendar
Zero-shot gains on LAMA, math, QA, MLQA, temporal tasks with perplexity preserved

method.summary: GPT-J is prompted with a few demonstrations per API to insert candidate calls into CCNet text; calls are executed and kept if they cut weighted cross-entropy on following tokens by at least tau_f; GPT-J is finetuned on the augmented text with a standard LM objective. At inference, decoding is interrupted at the arrow token, the API is called, and the result is inserted.
method.task: tool-augmented language modeling, zero-shot downstream evaluation

datasets.name: CCNet subset (C)
datasets.size: up to 25k examples per API (training); sizes in Table 2
datasets.split: 1,000-example CCNet dev set for checkpoint PPL
datasets.preprocessing: Per-tool heuristics: calculator needs >=3 numbers; calendar needs URL date (~18% of docs); MT keeps non-English chunk between English text, fastText confidence > 0.8, 10-token chunks

datasets.name: LAMA (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx)
datasets.preprocessing: drop examples where mask not final

datasets.name: MLQA
datasets.split: Es, De, Hi, Vi, Zh, Ar

other.api_tokens: ' [', ']', '->' used in place of <API>, </API>, arrow, no vocab change

other.used_for: scaling study, QA/calculator/Wikipedia search tools only

models.name: Atlas-large / Atlas-xxl
models.architecture: retrieval-augmented LM finetuned on Natural Questions

other.use: large for building C*, xxl at inference

training.warmup: linear warmup for first 10% of training
training.steps: up to 2k, evaluating PPL every 500 steps, best checkpoint kept

inference.decoding: greedy, but <API> started if among top k=10 tokens; at most one API call per input
inference.samples: single greedy run per item; no seeds stated
inference.prompting: prompted zero-shot, no in-context examples; prompts in Appendix C
inference.retrieval: Wikipedia BM25 over KILT dump; Atlas QA

metrics.name: Lenient match accuracy
metrics.definition: LAMA/TEMPLAMA/DATESET: correct word in first 5 words; QA: answer in first 20 words; MLQA: within 10 words; math: first number (or after '=') equals answer

metrics.name: Perplexity
metrics.definition: on WikiText and CCNet holdout, API calls disabled

eval.protocol: single run per model, no significance tests; Wikipedia search disabled on LAMA, QA tool disabled on QA datasets

prompts.text: Your task is to add calls to a Question Answering API to a piece of text. The questions should help you get information required to complete the text. You can call the API by writing "[QA(question)]" where "question" is the question you want to ask.
prompts.where: Fig 3, Appendix A.2 (truncated; few-shot examples follow)

prompts.text: Please complete the following text so that it is factually correct: x.

evidence.quote: a batch size of 128 and a learning rate of 1 · 10−5 with linear warmup for the first 10% of training

results.claim: Toolformer scores 40.4 on ASDiv with the calculator, vs 14.0 for GPT-3 175B and 14.8 with API calls disabled.
results.setup: Zero-shot prompted, greedy decoding with <API> started when in top k=10 tokens, at most one API call per input; GPT-J 6.7B finetuned on CCNet subset with API calls; metric: first number in output matches answer.
results.table: Table 4, row Toolformer, column ASDiv (GPT-3 14.0; Toolformer (disabled) 14.8)

results.setup: Zero-shot prompted, greedy decoding with <API> started when in top k=10 tokens, at most one API call per input; GPT-J 6.7B finetuned on CCNet subset with API calls
results.table: Table 4, row Toolformer, columns SVAMP 29.4, MAWPS 44.0

results.claim: Allowing API calls more than doubles math performance for all tasks; calculator is used on 97.9% of examples.
results.setup: Zero-shot prompted, greedy decoding with <API> started when in top k=10 tokens, at most one API call per input; GPT-J 6.7B finetuned on CCNet subset with API calls
results.quote: for 97.9% of all examples the model decides to ask the calculator tool for help

results.claim: Toolformer scores 53.5 on LAMA T-REx vs 39.8 for GPT-3 175B and 34.9 disabled; 33.8 SQuAD, 11.5 Google-RE.
results.setup: Zero-shot prompted, greedy decoding with <API> started when in top k=10 tokens, at most one API call per input; GPT-J 6.7B finetuned on CCNet subset with API calls; Wikipedia Search disabled for LAMA; correct if answer within first five words; examples with non-final mask removed.
results.table: Table 3, row Toolformer, column T-REx (GPT-3 39.8; Toolformer (disabled) 34.9)

results.claim: On LAMA the model asks the QA tool in almost all cases.
results.quote: the model independently decides to ask the question answering tool for the required information in almost all cases (98.1%)

results.claim: Toolformer improves over best same-size baseline by 11.7, 5.2 and 18.6 points on SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx.
results.quote: improving upon the best baseline by 11.7, 5.2 and 18.6 points, respectively

results.claim: On QA datasets Toolformer beats GPT-J baselines but falls short of GPT-3 175B (WebQS 26.3 vs 29.0; NQ 17.7 vs 22.6; TriviaQA 48.8 vs 65.9).
results.setup: WebQS, NQ, TriviaQA; QA tool disabled, Wikipedia search used 99.3%; correct if answer within first 20 words.
results.table: Table 5, row Toolformer, column WebQS (GPT-3 29.0; NQ 17.7 vs 22.6; TriviaQA 48.8 vs 65.9)

results.claim: Wikipedia search used on nearly all QA examples.
results.quote: mostly relying on the Wikipedia search API (99.3%)

results.claim: On DATESET Toolformer reaches 27.3 vs 5.9 disabled, due to calendar tool used on 54.8% of examples; on TEMPLAMA 16.3 and calendar used on only 0.2%.
results.table: Table 7, row Toolformer, columns TEMPLAMA 16.3, DATESET 27.3 (disabled 5.9; GPT-3 0.8)

results.claim: Calendar tool is used for 54.8% of DATESET examples.
results.quote: which it makes use of for 54.8% of all examples

results.claim: MLQA: translation tool helps Toolformer in all languages but it does not consistently beat vanilla GPT-J because CCNet finetuning hurts.
results.setup: MLQA, question in foreign language, English context; correct if within first 10 words; MT tool used for 63.8% to 94.9% except Hindi 7.3%.
results.table: Table 6, row Toolformer, column Es (GPT-J 15.2; De 13.5 vs 16.5)

results.claim: Finetuning on API-augmented data does not increase perplexity vs finetuning on plain CCNet (API calls disabled).

results.note: Perplexity with API calls enabled not measured (intractable).

results.claim: Tool use only emerges at around 775M parameters; smaller GPT-2 models gain nothing from tools, and a large gap remains for GPT-J.
results.setup: GPT-2 124M, 355M, 775M, 1.6B and GPT-J with QA, calculator, Wikipedia search only
results.quote: the ability to leverage the provided tools only emerges at around 775M parameters

results.claim: Raising k from 1 to 10 raises API-call rate on T-REx from 40.3% to 98.1% and on WebQS from 8.5% to 100%; T-REx accuracy 47.8 at k=1 to 53.5 at k=10.
results.setup: T-REx subset of LAMA and WebQS

results.claim: Number of API-call examples in C* at tau_f=1.0: QA 18,526; WikiSearch 60,974; Calculator 994; Calendar 20,587; MT 1,034.

limits: No chained tool use (calls generated independently)
No interactive tool use such as query reformulation or browsing results
Sensitive to input wording when deciding to call an API
Sample-inefficient: over a million documents yield only a few thousand useful calculator calls
Does not consider tool-dependent computational cost
Evaluation is lenient-match zero-shot, single run; perplexity with API calls enabled not computed

lineage.note: most closely related; similar self-supervised objective but only in downstream-finetuned settings (Parisi et al.)
Schick and Schütze 2021b; Honovich et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2022
